long: Ethereum mainnet launched with Frontier on July 30, 2015, as a blockchain that runs programs, not just payments. Since then it has gone through about 20 network upgrades, switched from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake at the Merge, and added a cheap data layer (blobs) for rollups. This series opens the hood one mechanism per post: accounts, gas, the EVM, consensus, staking and blobs, each with a source.
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #1: Ethereum mainnet (Frontier) launched July 30, 2015. Since then: about 20 network upgrades, a switch from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and a data layer for rollups. This series covers how each piece works, one fact per post.
simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #1: Ethereum went live on July 30, 2015, as a blockchain that runs programs, not just payments. This series opens the hood: accounts, gas, the EVM, staking, blobs. One mechanism a day.

card.title: A blockchain that runs programs
card.sub: About 20 upgrades since launch. One mechanism per post, each with a source.

long: Ethereum uses an account model, not Bitcoin's UTXO model. Bitcoin tracks unspent coins; Ethereum keeps a ledger of accounts whose balances go up and down. Each account has 4 fields: nonce, balance (in wei), storageRoot (root of its storage trie) and codeHash (hash of its code; for a plain wallet, the hash of empty code). This makes smart contracts with persistent state natural to express.
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #2: Ethereum uses an account model, not UTXOs. Each account holds 4 fields: nonce, balance (in wei), storageRoot (root of its storage trie) and codeHash (hash of its code; for wallets, the hash of empty code).
simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #2: Bitcoin tracks coins (unspent outputs). Ethereum tracks accounts, like a bank ledger: each address has a balance that goes up and down.

card.title: Accounts, not unspent coins
card.sub: Each account holds a nonce, a balance, a storage root and a code hash.

long: Ethereum has two account types. Externally owned accounts (EOAs) are controlled by a secp256k1 private key: that's your wallet. Contract accounts are controlled by their EVM code. Only EOAs can originate a transaction; a contract never acts on its own, it only runs when a transaction or another contract calls it. Every on-chain action therefore starts with a signature from a key holder.
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #3: Two account types: externally owned accounts (EOAs), controlled by a secp256k1 key, and contract accounts, controlled by EVM code. Only EOAs originate transactions; contracts run when called.
simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #3: Two kinds of accounts: ones controlled by a private key (your wallet) and ones controlled by code (smart contracts). Only key holders can start a transaction; contracts only react.

card.title: Two kinds of accounts
card.sub: Keys control wallets, code controls contracts. Only key holders start a transaction.

long: An Ethereum address is derived from the public key: take the 64-byte uncompressed secp256k1 public key (without the 0x04 prefix), hash it with Keccak-256 and keep the last 20 bytes. 20 bytes is 40 hex characters, the part after 0x.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #4: An Ethereum address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(public key), where the key is the 64-byte uncompressed secp256k1 point without the 0x04 prefix.

20 bytes = 40 hex characters, the part after 0x. Unlike Bitcoin, there's one address format per key, and no checksum in the raw bytes.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #4: Your Ethereum address is derived from your public key: hash it, keep the last 20 bytes. That's the 40 hex characters after 0x.

It's a one-way process: from the address, nobody can work back to your public key, let alone your private key. The address is just a short fingerprint.

card.title: Where your address comes from
card.sub: Hash the public key with Keccak-256 and keep the last 20 bytes: 40 hex characters.

long: EIP-55 adds a checksum to addresses using letter case. Hash the lowercase hex address with Keccak-256; each letter in the address is uppercased if the matching nibble of the hash is >= 8. A typo breaks the pattern with high probability, so wallets can catch it. The mixed case is not random. An all-lowercase address is still valid, it simply carries no checksum.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #5: EIP-55 checksum: hash the lowercase hex address with Keccak-256; each letter in the address is uppercased if the matching hash nibble is >= 8.

A typo breaks the pattern with high probability, so wallets can catch it. The mixed case isn't random. An all-lowercase address stays valid, it just carries no checksum.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #5: Ever noticed addresses mix UPPER and lower case letters? It's not random: the pattern is a checksum that lets wallets catch typos.

The capitals are computed from a hash of the address itself. Change one character, and the expected pattern no longer matches. An all-lowercase address still works, but without that safety net.

card.title: Mixed-case addresses are a checksum
card.sub: EIP-55 uses letter case to encode a hash, so wallets can catch typos.

long: Ethereum's keccak256 is not the NIST SHA3-256 standard. Both use the same Keccak permutation, but FIPS 202 changed the padding (domain byte 0x06 instead of Keccak's original 0x01), so the same input gives a different hash. Ethereum and Solidity's keccak256() use the original Keccak. Calling it 'SHA-3' is common but wrong, and mixing them up breaks signatures and addresses.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #6: Ethereum's keccak256 is not NIST SHA3-256. Both use the Keccak permutation, but FIPS 202 changed the padding (domain byte 0x06 vs Keccak's original 0x01), so the same input gives a different hash.

Ethereum and Solidity's keccak256() use the original Keccak. Calling it "SHA-3" is common but wrong, and mixing them breaks signatures and addresses.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #6: Ethereum's hash function is often called SHA-3, but it isn't the official SHA-3. It uses the original Keccak, so the same input gives a different hash.

Ethereum picked Keccak before the standard was finalized with a small change. A developer using the "official" SHA-3 library by mistake gets wrong addresses and broken signatures.

card.title: Keccak-256 is not official SHA-3
card.sub: Same permutation, different padding. The same input gives a different hash.

long: ETH units: 1 ETH = 10^18 wei, the smallest unit. 1 gwei = 10^9 wei, a billionth of an ETH, and is the usual unit for gas prices. Older named units: szabo (10^12 wei) and finney (10^15 wei). The protocol itself only knows wei: every balance and a transaction's value field are integers in wei, which avoids rounding errors.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #7: ETH units: 1 ETH = 10^18 wei, the smallest unit; 1 gwei = 10^9 wei, the usual unit for gas prices. Older named units: szabo (10^12 wei) and finney (10^15 wei).

The protocol itself only knows wei: every balance and a tx's value field are integers in wei, which avoids rounding errors.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #7: 1 ETH = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei, the smallest unit. Gas prices use gwei: one billionth of an ETH. Under the hood, every balance is counted in wei.

Whole numbers only, no decimals. That way, every node computes exactly the same balances, with no rounding differences between machines.

card.title: One ETH, counted in wei
card.sub: Gas prices use gwei, a billionth of an ETH. The protocol only knows wei.

long: An Ethereum transaction has no 'from' field. Nodes recover the signer's public key from the ECDSA signature (v, r, s) and derive the sender address from it. This saves space and means the sender can't be faked: whoever signed is the sender. The same recovery is available to contracts through the ecrecover precompile at address 0x01.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #8: There is no "from" field in an Ethereum transaction. Nodes recover the signer's public key from the ECDSA signature (v, r, s) and derive the sender address from it.

This saves space, and the sender can't be faked: whoever signed is the sender. Contracts get the same recovery through the ecrecover precompile at address 0x01.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #8: An Ethereum transaction has no "from" field. Nodes work out who sent it from the signature itself.

Only the real owner of a key could produce a signature that points back to their address. So the sender can't be faked, and every transaction saves 20 bytes of space.

card.title: No 'from' field in a transaction
card.sub: Nodes recover the sender from the signature. Whoever signed is the sender.

long: Each EOA has a nonce: the number of transactions it has sent. A transaction must carry exactly the account's current nonce, so transactions from one account run in strict order and an old signed transaction can't be replayed. Wallets 'speed up' or cancel a pending transaction by sending a new one with the same nonce and a higher fee.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #9: Each EOA has a nonce: the number of transactions it has sent. A tx must carry exactly the account's current nonce, so txs from one account run in strict order and an old signed tx can't be replayed.

Wallets "speed up" or cancel a pending tx by sending a new one with the same nonce and a higher fee.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #9: Every wallet has a counter called a nonce. Each transaction uses the next number, so the same transaction can't be replayed and order is guaranteed.

It also explains "stuck" transactions: if one with a low fee is pending, all your later ones wait behind it. Wallets fix it by resending that number with a higher fee.

card.title: The nonce keeps transactions in order
card.sub: Each transaction carries the next number, so old ones can't be replayed.

long: EIP-155 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) mixes the chain ID into the signed data, with v = chainId*2 + 35 or 36. A transaction signed for Ethereum mainnet (chain ID 1) is therefore invalid on Ethereum Classic or a testnet, which blocks cross-chain replay. Newer typed transactions carry chainId as an explicit field.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #10: EIP-155 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) mixes the chain ID into the signed data, with v = chainId*2 + 35 or 36.

A tx signed for mainnet (chain ID 1) is therefore invalid on Ethereum Classic or a testnet, which blocks cross-chain replay. Newer typed transactions carry chainId as an explicit field.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #10: Why can't a transaction signed for Ethereum be replayed on another chain? Since 2016, each signature includes the chain's ID. Ethereum mainnet is chain 1.

This mattered right after Ethereum and Ethereum Classic split: the same accounts existed on both, and a payment on one could be copied to the other.

card.title: Signatures bound to one chain
card.sub: Since EIP-155 in 2016, a mainnet transaction is invalid on other chains.

long: For every valid ECDSA signature (r, s) there is a twin (r, n-s) that is also valid. EIP-2 (Homestead, 2016) rejects transaction signatures with s > secp256k1n/2, so only the 'low' one is accepted. This removes signature malleability: nobody can tweak a signature to change a transaction's hash (its ID) without invalidating it.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #11: For every valid ECDSA signature (r, s) there's a twin (r, n-s) that's also valid. EIP-2 (Homestead, 2016) rejects tx signatures with s > secp256k1n/2, so only the "low" one is accepted.

This removes signature malleability: nobody can tweak a signature to change a tx's hash (its ID) without invalidating it.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #11: An ECDSA signature has a "mirror twin" that is also valid. Since 2016, Ethereum only accepts one of the two, so nobody can tweak a signature to change a transaction's ID.

Without that rule, anyone could flip a pending transaction's signature. It would still be valid, but with a new ID, which confuses apps that track payments by ID.

card.title: Every signature has a valid twin
card.sub: EIP-2 accepts only the low one, so nobody can tweak a transaction's ID.

long: Every EVM opcode has a gas cost, a measure of work. A transaction pays gas_used times the gas price. A plain ETH transfer costs the intrinsic 21,000 gas; contract calls cost more depending on what they do. The gas limit field caps what a transaction may use: if it runs out, its state changes are reverted but the gas spent is still paid.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #12: Every EVM opcode has a gas cost, a measure of work; a tx pays gas_used × gas price. A plain ETH transfer costs the intrinsic 21,000 gas; contract calls cost more depending on what they do.

The gas limit field caps what a tx may use: if it runs out, its state changes are reverted, but the gas spent is still paid.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #12: Every action on Ethereum costs "gas", a unit of work. A plain ETH transfer always costs 21,000 gas. Running a contract costs more, depending on what it does.

You also set a maximum. If the work needs more than that, everything is cancelled, but you still pay for the gas used: nodes did the work either way.

card.title: Gas measures every step of work
card.sub: A plain ETH transfer costs 21,000 gas. Contract calls cost more.

long: Block size is set by the block gas limit, which proposers vote on: each block may move it by less than 1/1024 of the parent's limit, so it changes in small steps. EIP-7935, written in April 2025 when mainnet was at 36M gas, had execution clients raise their default gas limit to 60M ahead of Fusaka (Dec 2025). No hard fork is needed for this.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #13: The block gas limit is voted by proposers: each block may move it by < 1/1024 of the parent's limit, so it changes in small steps.

EIP-7935, written in Apr 2025 with mainnet at 36M gas, had execution clients raise their default gas limit to 60M ahead of Fusaka (Dec 2025). No hard fork is needed for this.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #13: How big can a block be? Validators decide together: each new block can move the limit only a tiny step up or down. For Fusaka (Dec 2025), clients' default limit was raised to 60 million gas.

No network upgrade is needed: when enough validators run the new default, the limit climbs block by block until it gets there.

card.title: Block size is a vote
card.sub: Each block can move the gas limit by less than 1/1024. No hard fork needed.

long: At the Frontier launch (July 30, 2015) each block had a 5,000 gas limit, below the 21,000 gas a single transfer needs, so early blocks could hold no transactions. It let miners start and users set up clients without rushing. 'Frontier Thawing' at block 200,000 (Sep 7, 2015) lifted the limit and set a default gas price of 51 gwei.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #14: At the Frontier launch (July 30, 2015), each block had a 5,000 gas limit, below the 21,000 gas of a single transfer, so early blocks could hold no txs.

It let miners start and users set up clients without rushing. "Frontier Thawing" at block 200,000 (Sep 7, 2015) lifted the limit and set a default gas price of 51 gwei.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #14: Ethereum's first blocks were almost empty on purpose: at launch, each block was capped at 5,000 gas, not even enough for one transfer. The cap was lifted at block 200,000.

That gave miners time to start and users time to set up, before any real money moved. Five weeks later, in September 2015, the network was "thawed".

card.title: The first blocks were empty on purpose
card.sub: At launch a block couldn't fit one transfer. The cap was lifted at block 200,000.

long: EIP-1559 (London, Aug 5, 2021) gives each block a base fee that is burned, not paid to the block producer. The base fee moves by up to 12.5% per block: up if the parent used more gas than the target, down if it used less. Part of every fee since then is destroyed, and fees became more predictable.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #15: EIP-1559 (London, Aug 5, 2021): each block has a base fee that is burned, not paid to the block producer.

It moves by up to 12.5% per block: up if the parent used more gas than the target, down if it used less. Since then part of every fee is destroyed, and fees became more predictable.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #15: Since August 2021, part of every Ethereum fee is destroyed (burned). This "base fee" rises when blocks are more than half full and falls when they are less than half full.

Wallets can now predict fees much better, since the base fee changes by at most 12.5% per block. Only the tip on top goes to the validator.
variant:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #15: Part of every fee paid on Ethereum since 2021 has simply vanished, on purpose. EIP-1559 burns the "base fee" of every transaction instead of paying it to the block producer.

Validators only keep the small tip. The burned ETH is gone for good, and the busier the network, the more is burned.

card.title: Part of every fee is burned
card.sub: Since London in 2021, the base fee is destroyed instead of paid to the producer.

long: EIP-1559 type-2 transactions set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas. The price paid per gas is base fee + min(tip, maxFee - base fee). The base fee part is burned, the tip goes to the block proposer, and any margin between that and the max is never charged. Users can set a generous max without overpaying.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #16: EIP-1559 type-2 txs set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas. Effective price per gas = base fee + min(tip, maxFee - base fee).

The base fee part is burned, the tip goes to the block proposer, and any margin up to the max is never charged. Users can set a generous max without overpaying.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #16: With EIP-1559 you set a maximum price and a tip. You pay the network's current base fee plus your tip, never more than your max. The rest stays in your wallet.

So a high max isn't money wasted: it's a ceiling. If the base fee is lower when your transaction lands, you pay the lower price.

card.title: Set a max, pay only what's needed
card.sub: You pay base fee plus tip. The margin up to your max is never charged.

long: EIP-1559 uses an elasticity multiplier of 2: the gas target is half the gas limit, and a block can use up to twice the target. The base fee update is proportional to (gas_used - target) / target / 8, so a completely full block raises it by 12.5% and an empty one lowers it by 12.5%. Blocks aim to be half full; bursts are absorbed and the fee climbs until demand eases.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #17: EIP-1559 elasticity multiplier = 2: gas target = gas limit / 2, and a block can use up to 2x the target.

The base fee update is proportional to (gas_used - target) / target / 8, so a full block raises it 12.5% and an empty one lowers it 12.5%. Blocks aim to be half full; bursts are absorbed while the fee climbs.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #17: Ethereum blocks aim to be half full. Busy periods can fill them up to double that target, and the fee goes up until demand calms down.

A sudden rush doesn't instantly price everyone out: blocks stretch first. If the rush lasts, the fee rises a bit each block until enough people wait.

card.title: Blocks aim to be half full
card.sub: Bursts can fill up to twice the target, and the base fee climbs until demand eases.

long: EIP-2718 (Berlin, Apr 2021) introduced typed transaction envelopes: TransactionType || payload. The first byte says which format follows, so new kinds can be added without breaking old ones. Types today: 0 legacy, 1 access list (EIP-2930), 2 fee market (EIP-1559), 3 blob (EIP-4844), 4 set-code (EIP-7702).
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #18: EIP-2718 (Berlin, Apr 2021) introduced typed tx envelopes: TransactionType || payload. The first byte says which format follows, so new kinds can be added without breaking old ones.

Types today: 0 legacy, 1 access list (EIP-2930), 2 fee market (EIP-1559), 3 blob (EIP-4844), 4 set-code (EIP-7702).
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #18: Ethereum supports several transaction formats. Since 2021, the first byte of a transaction says which type it is, so new kinds can be added without breaking old ones.

Each upgrade added its own type: one for the new fee system, one for rollup data blobs, one for smart accounts. Old-style transactions still work alongside them.

card.title: The first byte names the format
card.sub: Typed envelopes let new transaction kinds arrive without breaking old ones.

long: EIP-2930 (Berlin) type-1 transactions can carry an access list of addresses and storage keys they will touch. Listed items are paid for up front, 2,400 gas per address and 1,900 per storage key, and are then treated as warm during execution, so later access uses the cheaper warm price. Declaring access in advance makes it a bit cheaper.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #19: EIP-2930 (Berlin) type-1 txs can carry an access list of addresses and storage keys they will touch.

Listed items are paid up front, 2,400 gas per address and 1,900 per storage key, and are then warm during execution, so later access uses the cheaper warm price. Declaring access in advance makes it a bit cheaper.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #19: A transaction can come with a list of the addresses and storage it will touch. Declaring them up front makes that access a bit cheaper.

It's like booking in advance: you pay a set price per item upfront, then each use during the transaction costs the low "already loaded" rate.

card.title: Declare your access up front
card.sub: An access list pre-warms addresses and storage keys, making that access a bit cheaper.

long: EIP-2929 (Berlin) made the first access to state in a transaction 'cold' and expensive: 2,100 gas for a storage slot (cold SLOAD) and 2,600 for an account. Later accesses in the same transaction are 'warm' at 100 gas. It was a response to DoS attacks that abused cheap state reads, which force nodes to hit disk.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #20: EIP-2929 (Berlin) made the first state access in a tx "cold" and expensive: 2,100 gas for a storage slot (cold SLOAD) and 2,600 for an account. Later accesses in the same tx are "warm" at 100 gas.

It was a response to DoS attacks that abused cheap state reads, which force nodes to hit disk.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #20: Reading contract data costs much more the first time in a transaction than the second time. The first read is "cold", later reads are "warm".

The first read may force nodes to fetch data from disk, which is slow. Attackers once abused cheap reads to slow the whole network, so the price now matches the real work.

card.title: Cold reads cost more than warm ones
card.sub: The first state access in a transaction is expensive. Later ones are cheap.

long: Transaction data (calldata) costs 4 gas per zero byte and 16 per non-zero byte. EIP-2028 (Istanbul, Dec 2019) cut the non-zero price from 68 to 16 gas, which made rollups posting their data to L1 much cheaper. Because zero bytes are cheaper, data with many zeros, like addresses with leading zeros, saves a little gas.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #21: Calldata costs 4 gas per zero byte and 16 per non-zero byte. EIP-2028 (Istanbul, Dec 2019) cut the non-zero price from 68 to 16 gas, which made rollups posting their data to L1 much cheaper.

Because zero bytes are cheaper, data with many zeros, like addresses with leading zeros, saves a little gas.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #21: Sending data inside a transaction costs gas per byte. Zero bytes are cheaper than non-zero bytes, which is why addresses with many leading zeros save a little.

A big price cut in 2019 made data four times cheaper, which helped the first rollups that post their transaction data to Ethereum.

card.title: Calldata got cheaper for rollups
card.sub: EIP-2028 cut the price of non-zero bytes. Zero bytes cost even less.

long: EIP-7623 (Pectra, May 2025) adds a calldata floor price: if a transaction spends little gas on execution, it pays at least 10 gas per zero byte and 40 per non-zero byte. Normal transactions are mostly unaffected, but data-heavy ones pay more. This caps the worst-case block size and pushes bulk data toward blobs.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #22: EIP-7623 (Pectra, May 2025) adds a calldata floor price: if a tx spends little gas on execution, it pays at least 10 gas per zero byte and 40 per non-zero byte.

Normal txs are mostly unaffected, but data-heavy ones pay more. This caps the worst-case block size and pushes bulk data toward blobs.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #22: Since Pectra (May 2025), transactions that mostly carry data and do little computing pay a higher minimum price. The goal: push bulk data toward blobs.

Regular users barely notice. But it stops anyone from stuffing blocks with cheap data, which keeps the worst-case block size under control.

card.title: A minimum price for data-heavy txs
card.sub: Since Pectra, transactions that mostly carry data pay more. Bulk data goes to blobs.

long: EIP-7825 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) caps the gas a single transaction can use at 16,777,216 (2^24), about 16.8 million. Blocks can keep growing, but heavy work must be split across transactions, so no single transaction can fill a whole block. This bounds worst-case validation time and helps future parallel execution.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #23: EIP-7825 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) caps the gas a single tx can use at 16,777,216 (2^24), ≈16.8M.

Blocks can keep growing, but heavy work must be split across txs, so no single tx can fill a whole block. This bounds worst-case validation time and helps future parallel execution.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #23: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), one transaction can't use more than about 16.8 million gas, however big blocks get. No single transaction can hog a whole block.

That also prepares for the future: many smaller transactions can be checked in parallel, while one giant one would have to run alone.

card.title: No transaction can fill a block
card.sub: Since Fusaka, one transaction is capped at about 16.8 million gas.

long: The EVM is a stack machine with 256-bit words and a maximum stack depth of 1024. Execution is deterministic: every node replays every transaction and must reach exactly the same state root, or it rejects the block. Same input, same result, on every machine, which is what lets thousands of nodes agree without trusting each other.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #24: The EVM is a stack machine with 256-bit words and a max stack depth of 1024. Execution is deterministic: every node replays every tx and must reach exactly the same state root, or it rejects the block.

Same input, same result on every machine, which is what lets thousands of nodes agree without trusting each other.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #24: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is a simple computer every node runs in exactly the same way. Same input, same result, on every machine on Earth.

That's the heart of Ethereum: thousands of computers run every transaction independently and must all get the same answer. If one doesn't, its result is rejected.

card.title: Same input, same result everywhere
card.sub: Every node replays every transaction and must reach exactly the same state root.

long: Each contract has its own storage: a map of 2^256 keys to 32-byte values. Writing a slot from zero to non-zero (SSTORE) costs 20,000 gas, plus 2,100 if the slot is cold, while a warm SLOAD costs 100. Writing new storage is one of the most expensive operations, so saving storage writes is the core of gas optimization.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #25: Each contract has its own storage: a map of 2^256 keys to 32-byte values. SSTORE from zero to non-zero costs 20,000 gas, plus 2,100 if the slot is cold, while a warm SLOAD is 100.

Writing new storage is one of the most expensive operations, so saving storage writes is the core of gas optimization.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #25: Each contract has its own giant key-value store with 2^256 slots. Writing a new value there is one of the most expensive things you can do on Ethereum.

Why so costly? Every node must keep that data for as long as it stays in storage. That's why good contracts store as little as possible and pack several values into one slot.

card.title: Storage writes are the big cost
card.sub: Each contract has 2^256 slots. Saving writes is the core of gas optimization.

long: EVM memory is a byte array that lives only for the duration of a call and is wiped afterwards. Its expansion cost is 3*words + words^2/512 (words of 32 bytes). The quadratic term means memory is cheap for a few KB but becomes prohibitive for many MB, which bounds how much memory a transaction can use.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #26: EVM memory is a byte array that lives only for the duration of a call and is wiped afterwards. Expansion cost = 3*words + words^2/512 (32-byte words).

The quadratic term makes memory cheap for a few KB but prohibitive for many MB, which bounds how much memory a tx can use.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #26: Contracts also get scratch memory that is wiped after each call. It's cheap at first, but the price climbs faster and faster as you use more of it.

A few kilobytes cost almost nothing. Many megabytes would cost more than a whole block allows. That keeps nodes safe from transactions that try to eat all their RAM.

card.title: Memory gets pricier as it grows
card.sub: Scratch memory is wiped after each call. Its cost is quadratic in size.

long: EIP-1153 (Dencun, March 2024) adds TSTORE and TLOAD: transient storage that persists across calls within one transaction and is cleared at its end. Each costs 100 gas, far below SSTORE. It is a third kind of contract memory between memory and storage, with typical uses like reentrancy locks and single-transaction token approvals.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #27: EIP-1153 (Dencun, March 2024) adds TSTORE and TLOAD: transient storage that persists across calls within one tx and is cleared at its end. Each costs 100 gas, far below SSTORE.

A third kind of contract memory, between memory and storage, with typical uses like reentrancy locks and single-tx token approvals.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #27: Since March 2024, contracts have a third kind of memory: data that lasts for a whole transaction, then disappears. Handy for locks against reentrancy attacks.

Before, such locks had to use permanent storage, which is expensive. Now they cost a fraction, and clean themselves up automatically.

card.title: Storage that lasts one transaction
card.sub: TSTORE and TLOAD clear at the end of the tx. Handy for reentrancy locks.

long: Clearing storage used to earn a large gas refund, so 'GasToken' schemes stored data when gas was cheap and cleared it when gas was expensive, effectively banking gas. EIP-3529 (London, 2021) removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund, lowered the SSTORE clearing refund and capped total refunds at gas_used/5 instead of /2. The trick became worthless.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #28: Clearing storage used to earn a large gas refund, so "GasToken" schemes stored data when gas was cheap and cleared it when gas was expensive, effectively banking gas.

EIP-3529 (London, 2021) removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund, lowered the SSTORE clear refund and capped refunds at gas_used/5 (was /2). The trick became worthless.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #28: Freeing storage used to earn back a big gas refund, so people "banked" gas in tokens when it was cheap. A 2021 change cut refunds and killed that trick.

The banking filled the blockchain with junk data just to be deleted later. Lower refunds removed the incentive, and with it a source of bloat.

card.title: How the gas banking trick died
card.sub: EIP-3529 cut storage refunds and capped them, so GasToken became worthless.

long: EIP-150 (Tangerine Whistle, Oct 2016): a CALL can forward at most 63/64 of the remaining gas. Each nested call keeps 1/64 back, so gas shrinks with depth, which made the attack that pushed calls to the 1024 call-depth limit impractical. The caller also always keeps some gas to handle a failed call.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #29: EIP-150 (Tangerine Whistle, Oct 2016): a CALL can forward at most 63/64 of the remaining gas. Each nested call keeps 1/64 back, so gas shrinks with depth.

That made the attack pushing calls to the 1024 call-depth limit impractical. The caller also always keeps some gas to handle a failed call.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #29: When a contract calls another, it can't hand over all its remaining gas: it always keeps a small part back. This rule stopped a whole family of attacks.

Attackers used to chain calls deep enough to make the victim's calls fail silently. Now, gas runs out long before that depth, and every caller can react to failures.

card.title: A call never gets all the gas
card.sub: Each nested call keeps 1/64 back. That stopped the call-depth attack.

long: REVERT (EIP-140, Byzantium, Oct 2017) lets a contract abort: it rolls back state changes, refunds the remaining gas and returns data such as an error reason. Before, the only ways to abort were running out of gas or hitting an invalid opcode, both of which burned all the gas. Failures became cheaper and easier to debug.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #30: REVERT (EIP-140, Byzantium, Oct 2017) lets a contract abort: it rolls back state changes, refunds remaining gas and returns data such as an error reason.

Before, the only ways to abort were running out of gas or an invalid opcode, both burning all the gas. Failures became cheaper and easier to debug.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #30: If a contract hits a problem, it can cancel everything it did and give back the gas it didn't use, along with a reason. Before 2017, a failure burned all the gas.

That's why your wallet can now tell you "insufficient balance" or "deadline passed" when a transaction fails, instead of a mysterious error.

card.title: Failing without burning all the gas
card.sub: Since 2017, REVERT rolls back changes, refunds unused gas and returns a reason.

long: STATICCALL (EIP-214, Byzantium) calls another contract in read-only mode: any state change (SSTORE, LOG, CREATE, value transfer, SELFDESTRUCT) makes the call fail. Solidity uses it for calls to view and pure functions. It lets a contract safely query another, for example for a price, knowing the callee can't modify anything.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #31: STATICCALL (EIP-214, Byzantium) calls another contract read-only: any state change (SSTORE, LOG, CREATE, value transfer, SELFDESTRUCT) makes the call fail. Solidity uses it for view and pure function calls.

A contract can safely query another, e.g. for a price, knowing the callee can't modify anything.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #31: Contracts can call others in "read-only" mode. If the called code tries to change anything, the call fails. Useful for price checks and views.

It's a safety guarantee: you can ask an unknown contract a question without letting it touch anything. Solidity uses it automatically for "view" functions.

card.title: Read-only calls between contracts
card.sub: With STATICCALL, any state change makes the call fail. Safe for price queries.

long: DELEGATECALL (EIP-7, Homestead) runs the target contract's code in the caller's context: same storage, same msg.sender and msg.value. A contract borrows another's code and runs it on its own data. It's the basis of libraries and proxy patterns such as EIP-1967 upgradeable proxies: the logic contract can be swapped while data stays in the proxy.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #32: DELEGATECALL (EIP-7, Homestead) runs the target's code in the caller's context: same storage, same msg.sender and msg.value. A contract borrows another's code and runs it on its own data.

It's the basis of libraries and proxy patterns like EIP-1967 upgradeable proxies: the logic can be swapped while data stays in the proxy.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #32: A contract can borrow another contract's code and run it on its own data. That's how "upgradeable" contracts work: the code can be swapped, the data stays.

Powerful, but risky: the borrowed code gets full access to the caller's storage. If it's buggy or malicious, the caller pays the price, as Parity users learned.

card.title: Borrow the code, keep the data
card.sub: DELEGATECALL runs another contract's code on your own storage. Proxies rely on it.

long: Nov 6, 2017: the shared library behind Parity multisig wallets was left uninitialized. A user called initWallet to become its owner, then kill(), which ran SELFDESTRUCT. The 587 wallets that relied on that library via DELEGATECALL froze 513,774.16 ETH, about 514,000 ETH, still stuck. A lesson on DELEGATECALL and initialization.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #33: Parity multisig, Nov 6, 2017: the shared library behind the wallets was left uninitialized. A user called initWallet to become its owner, then kill(), which ran SELFDESTRUCT.

The 587 wallets that relied on it via DELEGATECALL froze 513,774.16 ETH (≈514,000), still stuck. A lesson on DELEGATECALL and initialization.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #33: In Nov 2017, a user killed a shared library contract that hundreds of Parity wallets relied on. About 514,000 ETH has been stuck in those wallets ever since.

The library had never been set up, so anyone could claim it. Once it was deleted, the 587 wallets that borrowed its code could no longer move a single coin.

card.title: The Parity library kill switch
card.sub: One user killed a shared library in 2017. 587 wallets have been frozen since.

long: EIP-170 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) caps deployed contract code at 24,576 bytes (0x6000), about 24 KB. The limit bounds the DoS cost of loading code. It's why large protocols split their logic across several contracts, using libraries, proxies or the diamond pattern.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #34: EIP-170 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) caps deployed contract code at 24,576 bytes (0x6000), ≈24 KB. The limit bounds the DoS cost of loading code.

It's why large protocols split their logic across several contracts, using libraries, proxies or the diamond pattern.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #34: Smart contracts have a size limit: about 24 KB of code. Big apps have to split their logic across several contracts.

The limit protects nodes: loading huge code for every call would be an easy way to slow them down. Developers work around it with libraries and modular designs.

card.title: Contracts have a size limit
card.sub: EIP-170 caps deployed code, so big protocols split logic across contracts.

long: EIP-3860 (Shanghai, Apr 2023) limits initcode, the code that runs once to set up a new contract, to 49,152 bytes, twice the EIP-170 contract limit. It also charges 2 gas per 32-byte word of initcode, because nodes had to analyze it for jump destinations without being paid for that work.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #35: EIP-3860 (Shanghai, Apr 2023) limits initcode, the code that runs once to set up a new contract, to 49,152 bytes, twice the EIP-170 limit.

It also charges 2 gas per 32-byte word of initcode, because nodes had to analyze it for jump destinations without being paid for that work.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #35: The code that sets up a new contract also has a size limit, double the contract limit, and it's charged per chunk.

Nodes have to scan that setup code before running it. Before 2023 that scan was free, which was an opening for abuse. Now it has a price and a cap.

card.title: Setup code has a limit too
card.sub: EIP-3860 caps initcode at twice the contract limit and charges per 32-byte word.

long: EIP-3541 (London, 2021) rejects any new contract code that starts with the byte 0xEF. It reserved that prefix so future formats of contract code could be told apart from legacy code, originally for EOF (EVM Object Format). It was later used for EIP-7702 delegation designators, which begin with 0xef0100.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #36: EIP-3541 (London, 2021) rejects any new contract code starting with the byte 0xEF. It reserved that prefix so future code formats could be told apart from legacy code, originally for EOF (EVM Object Format).

It was later used for EIP-7702 delegation designators, which begin with 0xef0100.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #36: Since 2021, no new contract can start with the byte 0xEF. That byte is reserved so future versions of contract code can be told apart.

It's a marker for "this isn't old-style code". Since 2025, smart accounts use it to show that a normal wallet has delegated to a contract.

card.title: One byte reserved for the future
card.sub: New code can't start with 0xEF, kept for new formats and EIP-7702 delegations.

long: Contracts deployed with CREATE get the address: last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(RLP([sender, nonce])). For an EOA, the nonce is its transaction count; for a contract, the number of contracts it has created. So a contract's address can be computed before it exists, but it depends on deployment order.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #37: CREATE address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(RLP([sender, nonce])). For an EOA, the nonce is its tx count; for a contract, the number of contracts it has created.

So a contract's address can be computed before it exists, but it depends on deployment order: one extra transaction before deploying changes it.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #37: You can know a contract's address before it exists: it's computed from the creator's address and its nonce, for a normal wallet the number of transactions it has sent so far.

The catch: send one extra transaction first and the number changes, so the address changes too. A newer method fixes that.

card.title: An address known before it exists
card.sub: CREATE derives it from the creator's address and nonce, so order matters.

long: CREATE2 (EIP-1014, Constantinople, Feb 2019) computes the address as the last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(0xff ++ sender ++ salt ++ Keccak-256(init_code)). It depends on the salt and code, not on the nonce, so the address is known in advance whatever happens in between. Used for counterfactual wallets that receive funds before deployment, and same addresses on many chains.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #38: CREATE2 (EIP-1014, Constantinople, Feb 2019): address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(0xff ++ sender ++ salt ++ Keccak-256(init_code)). It depends on salt and code, not the nonce.

So the address is known in advance whatever happens in between. Used for counterfactual wallets that receive funds before deployment, and same addresses on many chains.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #38: Since 2019, a contract can be deployed to an address chosen in advance, whatever happens in between. Used for counterfactual wallets and same addresses on many chains.

A smart wallet can receive funds before it even exists on-chain, and only be deployed when first needed. That saves fees for new users.

card.title: Deploy to an address chosen in advance
card.sub: CREATE2 uses a salt and the code, not the nonce. Same address on many chains.

long: EIP-6780 (Dencun, March 2024) neutered SELFDESTRUCT: it only deletes a contract's code and storage if called in the same transaction that created it. Otherwise it just sends the contract's ETH to the target and the code stays. This ended 'metamorphic contracts' that used SELFDESTRUCT plus CREATE2 to redeploy different code at the same address.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #39: EIP-6780 (Dencun, March 2024) neutered SELFDESTRUCT: it only deletes a contract's code and storage if called in the same tx that created it. Otherwise it just sends the contract's ETH to the target and the code stays.

This ended "metamorphic contracts" that used SELFDESTRUCT + CREATE2 to redeploy different code at the same address.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #39: Contracts used to be able to delete themselves. Since March 2024, that only works in the same transaction that created them. Otherwise, the ETH is sent away but the code stays.

This closed a nasty trick: delete a contract, then deploy different code at the same address. Users could no longer trust that code wouldn't change.

card.title: SELFDESTRUCT lost its teeth
card.sub: Since 2024 it deletes code only in the creating tx. Metamorphic contracts are over.

long: A contract call names its function with a selector: the first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the function signature, e.g. transfer(address,uint256) = 0xa9059cbb. The arguments follow, ABI-encoded in 32-byte words. With only 32 bits, two different signatures can share a selector, so clashes are possible.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #40: A contract call names its function with a selector: the first 4 bytes of Keccak-256 of the function signature, e.g. transfer(address,uint256) = 0xa9059cbb. The arguments follow, ABI-encoded in 32-byte words.

With only 32 bits, two different signatures can share a selector, so clashes are possible.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #40: How does a contract know which function you're calling? The first 4 bytes of your transaction data name it, derived from a hash of the function's name.

For example, every ERC-20 transfer call starts with 0xa9059cbb. Wallets use these codes to show you what a transaction does, before you sign it.

card.title: Four bytes pick the function
card.sub: The selector is a hash prefix of the function signature. Clashes are possible.

long: Contracts emit events with LOG0-LOG4. Each log goes to the transaction receipt with up to 4 indexed 32-byte topics; topic 0 is usually the hash of the event signature. Each block header has a 2048-bit logs bloom filter for quick searching. Wallets and explorers read events to show history, but contracts themselves can't read logs.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #41: Contracts emit events with LOG0-LOG4. Each log goes to the tx receipt with up to 4 indexed 32-byte topics; topic 0 is usually the event signature hash.

Each block header has a 2048-bit logs bloom filter for quick searching. Wallets and explorers read events to show history, but contracts themselves can't read logs.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #41: When a contract does something worth noticing (a transfer, a swap), it can emit an "event". Wallets and explorers read these events to show your history.

Events are cheap because they're stored outside the contract's memory. The trade-off: contracts can't read them back, only apps outside the chain can.

card.title: Events tell wallets what happened
card.sub: Logs carry up to 4 indexed topics. Contracts can't read them, explorers can.

long: Precompiles are built-in contracts at low addresses that do heavy cryptography natively, much cheaper than EVM code: 0x01 ecrecover, 0x02 SHA-256, 0x03 RIPEMD-160, 0x04 identity, 0x05 modexp, 0x06-0x08 BN254 operations, 0x09 BLAKE2f, 0x0a KZG point evaluation, 0x0b-0x11 BLS12-381, and 0x100 for secp256r1 (P-256) verification.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #42: Precompiles are built-in contracts at low addresses doing heavy cryptography natively, much cheaper than EVM code: 0x01 ecrecover, 0x02 SHA-256, 0x03 RIPEMD-160, 0x04 identity, 0x05 modexp.

Then 0x06-0x08 BN254 ops, 0x09 BLAKE2f, 0x0a KZG point evaluation, 0x0b-0x11 BLS12-381, and 0x100 for secp256r1 (P-256) verification.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #42: Some built-in contracts live at tiny addresses like 0x01. They do heavy cryptography natively, much cheaper than writing it in contract code.

Checking a signature, hashing data, verifying a zero-knowledge proof: written in normal contract code, these would cost a fortune in gas. Built in, they're affordable.

card.title: Built-in crypto at tiny addresses
card.sub: Precompiles run heavy cryptography natively, far cheaper than EVM code.

long: Byzantium (Oct 2017) added precompiles for the BN254 (alt_bn128) curve at 0x06-0x08: point addition and scalar multiplication (EIP-196) and a pairing check (EIP-197). That is enough to verify Groth16 zk-SNARKs on-chain, which made zero-knowledge proofs practical on Ethereum. Istanbul later cut their gas cost (EIP-1108).
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #43: Byzantium (Oct 2017) added precompiles for the BN254 (alt_bn128) curve at 0x06-0x08: point addition and scalar multiplication (EIP-196) and a pairing check (EIP-197).

That's enough to verify Groth16 zk-SNARKs on-chain, which made zero-knowledge proofs practical on Ethereum. Istanbul later cut their gas cost (EIP-1108).
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #43: Zero-knowledge proofs on Ethereum became practical in 2017, when built-in operations for a special elliptic curve were added. Many zk apps still rely on them.

Privacy apps and zk-rollups both need to check these proofs on-chain. A 2019 upgrade then made them several times cheaper to use.

card.title: The curve that brought zk to Ethereum
card.sub: BN254 precompiles from 2017 made verifying Groth16 zk-SNARKs practical on-chain.

long: EIP-2537 (Pectra, May 2025) adds BLS12-381 precompiles at 0x0b-0x11: G1/G2 addition and multi-scalar multiplication, a pairing check and map-to-curve. Per the EIP, it gives 120+ bits of security vs 80 bits for the older BN254 precompile. It's the curve validators sign with, so contracts can verify consensus-layer signatures cheaply.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #44: EIP-2537 (Pectra, May 2025) adds BLS12-381 precompiles at 0x0b-0x11: G1/G2 addition and multi-scalar multiplication, a pairing check and map-to-curve.

Per the EIP: 120+ bits of security vs 80 bits for the older BN254 precompile. It's the curve validators sign with, so contracts can verify consensus-layer signatures cheaply.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #44: Since May 2025, contracts can natively check BLS signatures, the same kind Ethereum validators use. That makes it cheaper to verify the consensus layer from inside a contract.

It's also a stronger curve than the one added in 2017. Bridges, staking apps and new zero-knowledge systems can all build on it.

card.title: Contracts can check BLS signatures
card.sub: EIP-2537 adds the validators' curve, so consensus signatures verify cheaply.

long: EIP-7951 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) adds a precompile that verifies secp256r1 (P-256) signatures. P-256 is the curve used by FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys, Apple's Secure Enclave and Android Keystore. Smart wallets can now verify signatures from phone secure chips and passkeys cheaply, a step toward wallets unlocked with Face ID.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #45: EIP-7951 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) adds a precompile verifying secp256r1 (P-256) signatures. P-256 is the curve of FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys, Apple's Secure Enclave and Android Keystore.

Smart wallets can now verify signatures from phone secure chips and passkeys cheaply, a step toward wallets unlocked with Face ID.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #45: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), Ethereum can check signatures from phone secure chips and passkeys natively. A step toward wallets you unlock with Face ID.

Your phone already holds a secure key for passkey logins. Now a smart wallet can use that same key, which makes passkey-based wallets possible (recovery still matters).

card.title: Passkeys meet smart wallets
card.sub: Fusaka adds native P-256 checks: phone secure chips and passkeys, verified cheaply.

long: PUSH0 (EIP-3855, Shanghai, 2023) pushes the value 0 on the stack for 2 gas and 1 byte. Before, compilers used PUSH1 0x00 (3 gas, 2 bytes) or tricks like RETURNDATASIZE. Zero is pushed constantly, so this small instruction saves gas and bytes in almost every contract. Solidity targets it by default since 0.8.20.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #46: PUSH0 (EIP-3855, Shanghai, 2023) pushes 0 on the stack for 2 gas and 1 byte. Before, compilers used PUSH1 0x00 (3 gas, 2 bytes) or tricks like RETURNDATASIZE.

Zero is pushed constantly, so this small instruction saves gas and bytes in almost every contract. Solidity has targeted it by default since 0.8.20.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #46: Sometimes small things matter: in 2023 the EVM got an instruction that just pushes the number zero. It saves a little gas in almost every contract.

Zero is used everywhere in code. Saving one byte and one unit of gas each time adds up across millions of transactions.

card.title: An opcode that just pushes zero
card.sub: PUSH0 saves gas and a byte in almost every contract. Solidity uses it by default.

long: EIP-7939 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) adds the CLZ opcode: count the leading zero bits of a 256-bit word, returning 256 for 0. Before, contracts used costly bit-by-bit loops or tricks. It speeds up math libraries (log2, sqrt, fixed-point math) and compression code.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #47: EIP-7939 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) adds the CLZ opcode: count the leading zero bits of a 256-bit word, returning 256 for 0.

Before, contracts used costly bit-by-bit loops or tricks. It speeds up math libraries (log2, sqrt, fixed-point math) and compression code, which DeFi protocols use heavily.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #47: Fusaka (Dec 2025) added a new EVM instruction that counts leading zero bits in a number. Useful for math libraries and compression.

It sounds obscure, but DeFi apps compute logarithms and square roots all the time. One native instruction replaces long, expensive loops.

card.title: Counting leading zeros natively
card.sub: Fusaka's CLZ opcode replaces bit-by-bit loops in log2, sqrt and fixed-point math.

long: The BLOCKHASH opcode only returns hashes of the 256 most recent blocks, 0 otherwise. EIP-2935 (Pectra, May 2025) also stores the last 8,191 block hashes in a system contract's storage. Contracts and stateless clients can then prove facts against older blocks.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #48: BLOCKHASH only returns hashes of the 256 most recent blocks (0 otherwise). EIP-2935 (Pectra, May 2025) also stores the last 8,191 block hashes in a system contract's storage.

Contracts and stateless clients can then prove facts against older blocks, about 27 hours back instead of 51 minutes.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #48: Contracts could only see the IDs of the last 256 blocks, about 51 minutes of history. Since Pectra (May 2025), the last 8,191 block IDs are kept in a special contract.

That's about 27 hours of history. Contracts can now check proofs about older blocks, which helps bridges and light clients.

card.title: Contracts can see further back
card.sub: BLOCKHASH covers only 256 blocks. EIP-2935 keeps older hashes in a system contract.

long: EIP-4399 (Paris, the Merge) repurposed the DIFFICULTY opcode (0x44) as PREVRANDAO, which returns the beacon chain's RANDAO mix. It gives contracts a random-looking value, but a proposer can only publish or skip its block, giving it about 1 bit of influence. Useful, but not safe on its own for high-value lotteries.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #49: EIP-4399 (Paris, the Merge) repurposed the DIFFICULTY opcode (0x44) as PREVRANDAO, returning the beacon chain's RANDAO mix.

It gives contracts a random-looking value, but a proposer can publish or skip its block, so it gets ≈1 bit of influence. Useful, but not safe on its own for high-value lotteries.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #49: Contracts can get a random-looking number from the consensus layer since the Merge. It's useful but not perfect: a block proposer can bias it slightly.

The proposer can't pick the number, but it can choose not to publish its block if it dislikes the result. For a big lottery, that small edge could be worth a lot.

card.title: Randomness with a small catch
card.sub: PREVRANDAO gives a random-looking value, but proposers can bias it slightly.

long: EIP-4788 (Dencun, March 2024) stores the parent beacon block root in a system contract, in a ring buffer of 8,191 entries. Contracts can then verify Merkle proofs of beacon state, such as balances, withdrawals or validator status, against it. Staking apps can check validator data without trusting an oracle.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #50: EIP-4788 (Dencun, March 2024) stores each parent beacon block root in a system contract, in a ring buffer of 8,191 entries.

Contracts can verify Merkle proofs of beacon state against it: balances, withdrawals, validator status. Staking apps can check validator data without trusting an oracle.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #50: Since March 2024, contracts can read a fingerprint of the consensus layer's latest blocks. That lets staking apps check validator data without trusting an oracle.

Before, a staking app had to rely on someone reporting validator balances. Now it can verify a proof directly against data the chain itself provides.

card.title: Reading the beacon chain from a contract
card.sub: EIP-4788 stores beacon roots, so staking apps can verify data without an oracle.

long: Ethereum stores its state in a Merkle Patricia Trie, keyed by Keccak-256(address). Each block header commits to a stateRoot, transactionsRoot and receiptsRoot: one 32-byte fingerprint summarizes every balance and contract, and changing anything changes it completely. Any account can be proven against a header with a Merkle proof.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #51: Ethereum stores its state in a Merkle Patricia Trie keyed by Keccak-256(address). Each header commits to a stateRoot, transactionsRoot and receiptsRoot.

One 32-byte fingerprint summarizes every balance and contract, and changing anything changes it completely. Any account can be proven against a header with a Merkle proof.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #51: The whole state of Ethereum (every balance and contract) is summarized by one 32-byte fingerprint in each block header. Change one balance and it changes completely.

That's what lets light wallets check your balance without downloading everything: a short proof links your account to the fingerprint in a trusted header.

card.title: One fingerprint for the whole state
card.sub: Change one balance and the state root changes completely. Any account can be proven.

long: RLP (Recursive Length Prefix) is the execution layer's serialization format. It encodes only byte strings and nested lists; everything else is built from those. The first byte's range says what follows: 0x00-0x7f a single byte, 0x80-0xbf a string, 0xc0-0xff a list. The consensus layer uses a different format, SSZ.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #52: RLP (Recursive Length Prefix) is the execution layer's serialization format. It encodes only byte strings and nested lists; everything else is built from those.

The first byte's range says what follows: 0x00-0x7f a single byte, 0x80-0xbf a string, 0xc0-0xff a list. The consensus layer uses a different format, SSZ.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #52: Ethereum has its own simple way to turn data into bytes, called RLP. It only knows two things: strings of bytes and lists. Everything else is built from those.

The first byte tells the reader what's coming: one byte, a string, or a list, and how long. The consensus side of Ethereum uses a different format.

card.title: RLP knows only two things
card.sub: Byte strings and lists. Everything else on the execution layer is built from those.

long: In June 2016 The DAO, a huge investment contract, was drained via a reentrancy bug of about 3.6M ETH. The DAO fork at block 1,920,000 (Jul 20, 2016) moved its funds to a contract with a single withdraw function so holders could get ETH back. Miners and users who rejected rewriting history kept the old chain running: Ethereum Classic.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #53: In June 2016, The DAO, a huge investment contract, was drained via a reentrancy bug of ≈3.6M ETH. The DAO fork at block 1,920,000 (Jul 20, 2016) moved its funds to a contract with a single withdraw function.

Holders got their ETH back. Miners and users who rejected rewriting history kept the old chain running: Ethereum Classic.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #53: In June 2016, a hacker drained ETH from The DAO, a huge investment contract. Ethereum chose to rewrite history to return the funds. Those who refused kept the old chain: Ethereum Classic.

About 3.6 million ETH was at stake. The split still divides opinion: some saw a rescue, others a break with "code is law".

card.title: The DAO hack and the fork
card.sub: Ethereum rewrote history to return funds. Those who refused kept Ethereum Classic.

long: The difficulty bomb (Ice Age) added an exponentially growing term to proof-of-work difficulty, to make mining harder over time and force the move to proof-of-stake. It was delayed several times: EIP-649 (Byzantium), EIP-1234, EIP-2384 (Muir Glacier), EIP-3554, EIP-4345 (Arrow Glacier) and EIP-5133 (Gray Glacier), until the Merge made it irrelevant.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #54: The difficulty bomb (Ice Age) added an exponentially growing term to PoW difficulty, to make mining harder over time and force the move to proof-of-stake.

It was delayed by EIP-649 (Byzantium), EIP-1234, EIP-2384 (Muir Glacier), EIP-3554, EIP-4345 (Arrow Glacier) and EIP-5133 (Gray Glacier), until the Merge made it irrelevant.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #54: Ethereum had a built-in "bomb" that made mining harder and harder over time, to force the move to proof-of-stake. It was pushed back several times before the Merge.

Each time proof-of-stake wasn't ready, an upgrade delayed the bomb. It worked as a deadline: nobody could just keep mining forever on the old system.

card.title: A bomb set to force proof-of-stake
card.sub: The difficulty bomb made mining ever harder. It was delayed several times until the Merge.

long: Before the Merge, Ethereum was mined with Ethash. Each hash reads pseudo-random pages from a multi-GB dataset, the DAG, which grew every epoch of 30,000 blocks. Memory bandwidth, not raw compute, was the bottleneck: the design aimed to let ordinary GPUs compete with specialized mining machines.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #55: Before the Merge, Ethereum was mined with Ethash: each hash reads pseudo-random pages from a multi-GB dataset, the DAG, which grew every epoch of 30,000 blocks.

Memory bandwidth, not raw compute, was the bottleneck: the design aimed to let ordinary GPUs compete with specialized mining machines.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #55: Before 2022, Ethereum was mined. Its mining algorithm needed lots of memory on purpose, so ordinary graphics cards could compete with specialized machines.

Each attempt had to read random pieces of a multi-gigabyte dataset. Specialized chips are great at raw math, but memory speed limited everyone about equally.

card.title: Mining built to favor GPUs
card.sub: Ethash read a multi-GB dataset, so memory bandwidth was the bottleneck, not compute.

long: The proof-of-work block reward fell over time: 5 ETH from genesis, 3 ETH at Byzantium (EIP-649, Oct 2017), 2 ETH at Constantinople (EIP-1234, Feb 2019). At the Merge (Sep 2022) mining stopped and rewards moved to validators on the beacon chain.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #56: The PoW block reward fell over time: 5 ETH from genesis, 3 ETH at Byzantium (EIP-649, Oct 2017), 2 ETH at Constantinople (EIP-1234, Feb 2019).

At the Merge (Sep 2022), mining stopped and rewards moved to validators on the beacon chain, paid for attesting and proposing.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #56: Miners' reward per block fell over time: 5 ETH at launch, then 3 ETH in 2017, then 2 ETH in 2019. After the Merge, mining rewards stopped completely.

The cuts came alongside delays of the difficulty bomb. Since the Merge, new ETH goes to validators instead, for voting on and proposing blocks.

card.title: Mining rewards shrank over time
card.sub: Byzantium and Constantinople cut the block reward. The Merge ended mining.

long: Proof-of-work Ethereum rewarded ommers (uncles): valid blocks that lost the race but were referenced by a later block within 6 generations. Rewarding them lowered the edge of large, well-connected mining pools. Proof-of-stake removed them; the ommersHash header field is now a constant.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #57: PoW Ethereum rewarded ommers (uncles): valid blocks that lost the race but were referenced by a later block within 6 generations.

Rewarding them lowered the edge of large, well-connected mining pools. Proof-of-stake removed them; the ommersHash header field is now a constant.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #57: In the mining days, a valid block that lost the race still earned a reward if a later block mentioned it. These were called uncle blocks.

Without them, small miners far from the big pools would lose more races and earn less. The rewards kept mining fairer. They disappeared with the Merge.

card.title: Uncle blocks still got paid
card.sub: Valid blocks that lost the race earned a reward, cutting the edge of big pools.

long: The Beacon Chain, Ethereum's proof-of-stake chain, launched on Dec 1, 2020 after the deposit contract reached its minimum of 16,384 deposits of 32 ETH. For almost 2 years it ran in parallel with proof-of-work mainnet, only coming to consensus on itself, until the Merge in Sep 2022 joined them.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #58: Beacon Chain genesis: Dec 1, 2020, after the deposit contract reached its minimum of 16,384 deposits of 32 ETH.

For almost 2 years it ran in parallel with PoW mainnet, only coming to consensus on itself, with no user transactions, until the Merge in Sep 2022 joined them.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #58: Ethereum's proof-of-stake chain started on Dec 1, 2020, running alongside the mined chain for almost 2 years. It needed 16,384 validators of 32 ETH each to start.

During that time it carried no user transactions: it only practiced agreeing with itself. Then, in Sep 2022, the two chains merged.

card.title: The Beacon Chain waited for its quorum
card.sub: It launched on Dec 1, 2020 and ran alongside the mined chain for almost 2 years.

long: Every validator starts with a deposit to one contract, 0x00000000219ab540356cBB839Cbe05303d7705Fa, deployed Oct 14, 2020 at block 11,052,984; its address starts with eight zeros. The contract keeps an incremental Merkle tree of deposits, which the consensus layer reads to create validators.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #59: Every validator starts with a deposit to one contract: 0x00000000219ab540356cBB839Cbe05303d7705Fa, deployed Oct 14, 2020 at block 11,052,984.

Its address starts with eight zeros. It keeps an incremental Merkle tree of deposits, which the consensus layer reads to create validators.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #59: Every Ethereum validator starts with a deposit to one contract, deployed on Oct 14, 2020. Its address starts with eight zeros: 0x00000000219ab5...

A staker calls its deposit function with 32 ETH, the validator's public key, withdrawal credentials and a signature, and the consensus layer creates the validator. It's one of the largest ETH holders on the network.

card.title: One contract starts every validator
card.sub: The deposit contract's address begins with eight zeros. Deployed Oct 14, 2020.

long: The Merge was not set at a block number or a date. It was triggered by a Terminal Total Difficulty of 58,750,000,000,000,000,000,000: the first proof-of-work block whose cumulative difficulty passed it became the last proof-of-work block. A block-height trigger could have been gamed: an attacker with a minority of hash power could build a fork reaching that height.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #60: The Merge wasn't set at a block number or a date. It was triggered by a Terminal Total Difficulty of 58,750,000,000,000,000,000,000: the first PoW block whose cumulative difficulty passed it became the last PoW block.

A block-height trigger could have been gamed by a minority-hashrate fork reaching that height first.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #60: The Merge wasn't set for a block number or a date. It was triggered when the total mining work ever done on Ethereum crossed a fixed threshold.

Why? A block number could be reached by a cheap fake chain of easy blocks. Total work can't be faked: you'd need the real computing power.

card.title: The Merge had no date or block number
card.sub: It fired when total mining difficulty crossed a fixed threshold, harder to game.

long: Paris, the Merge, happened on Sep 15, 2022: block 15,537,394 was the first execution block produced under proof-of-stake, without stopping the chain. EIP-3675 removed the proof-of-work validity rules, and the Engine API let the beacon chain's consensus client drive the execution client.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #61: Paris (the Merge), Sep 15, 2022: block 15,537,394 was the first execution block produced under PoS, without stopping the chain.

EIP-3675 removed the PoW validity rules, and the Engine API let the beacon chain's consensus client drive the execution client.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #61: On Sep 15, 2022, Ethereum switched from miners to stakers without stopping. Block 15,537,394 was the first one produced by proof-of-stake.

Often compared to changing a plane's engine mid-flight. Balances, contracts and apps all carried on as if nothing happened.

card.title: Switching engines without stopping
card.sub: Block 15,537,394 was the first one produced under proof-of-stake.

long: According to ethereum.org, citing a CCRI estimate, moving from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake cut Ethereum's annualized electricity use by more than 99.98%. Validating needs ordinary computers, not warehouses of mining rigs: security now comes from ETH at stake that can be slashed, not from electricity spent on hashing.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #62: Per ethereum.org, citing a CCRI estimate, moving from PoW to PoS cut Ethereum's annualized electricity use by more than 99.98%.

Validating needs ordinary computers, not warehouses of mining rigs. Security now comes from ETH at stake that can be slashed, not from electricity spent on hashing.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #62: The Merge cut Ethereum's energy use by more than 99.98%. Validating with staked ETH needs ordinary computers, not warehouses of mining rigs.

Security didn't disappear, it changed form: instead of burning electricity, validators put their own ETH at risk, and cheaters lose it.

card.title: The Merge's energy cut
card.sub: Security now comes from ETH at stake that can be slashed, not from electricity.

long: Since the Merge, an Ethereum node is two programs: an execution client (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth...) that runs transactions and contracts, and a consensus client (Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar, Grandine) that agrees with other nodes on the next block. They talk via the authenticated Engine API.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #63: Since the Merge, a node is two programs: an execution client (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth...) runs transactions and contracts.

A consensus client (Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar, Grandine) agrees with other nodes on the next block. The two talk via the authenticated Engine API.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #63: An Ethereum node is two programs working together: one runs transactions and contracts, the other agrees with other nodes on which block comes next.

Several teams write each half, in different languages. Node operators can mix and match, which keeps the network from depending on any one team.

card.title: A node is two programs
card.sub: One runs transactions, the other agrees on the next block. They talk via Engine API.

long: Beacon chain time is split into slots and epochs: SECONDS_PER_SLOT = 12 and SLOTS_PER_EPOCH = 32, so an epoch lasts 384 s, or 6.4 min. Each slot gives one proposer the chance to publish a block. If the proposer is offline the slot stays empty; the chain doesn't wait.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #64: Beacon chain time: SECONDS_PER_SLOT = 12, SLOTS_PER_EPOCH = 32, so an epoch lasts 384 s = 6.4 min. Each slot gives one proposer the chance to publish a block.

If the proposer is offline, the slot stays empty; the chain doesn't wait. Missed slots are normal and visible on explorers.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #64: Ethereum time runs in 12-second "slots", each with a chance for one block. 32 slots make an "epoch" of 6.4 minutes.

If the validator chosen for a slot is offline, that slot simply stays empty and the clock moves on. That's why blocks come every 12 seconds, give or take a missed one.

card.title: Slots and epochs set the clock
card.sub: 32 slots make an epoch of 6.4 minutes. Empty slots don't stop the chain.

long: Casper FFG gives finality. An epoch checkpoint is justified when attestations representing 2/3 of total stake vote for it, and finalized when the next checkpoint is justified on top of it. That typically takes about 2 epochs (12.8 min). Reverting a finalized block would require destroying a huge amount of staked ETH.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #65: Casper FFG finality: an epoch checkpoint is justified when attestations representing 2/3 of total stake vote for it, and finalized when the next checkpoint is justified on top of it.

That typically takes ≈2 epochs (12.8 min). Reverting a finalized block would require destroying a huge amount of staked ETH.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #65: On Ethereum, a block becomes "final" (cannot be reversed without destroying a huge amount of staked ETH) after about 13 minutes.

It takes two rounds of votes from two-thirds of all stake. Before that, a block is very likely to stay, but not yet guaranteed. Exchanges often wait for finality.

card.title: When a block becomes final
card.sub: Casper FFG needs votes from 2/3 of stake. Undoing it would destroy huge stake.

long: Ethereum's fork choice rule is LMD-GHOST: starting from the last justified checkpoint, at each fork follow the branch with the most weight from each validator's latest attestation. It picks the head of the chain every slot. Gasper is the combination of LMD-GHOST with Casper FFG finality.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #66: Fork choice is LMD-GHOST: from the last justified checkpoint, at each fork follow the branch with the most weight from each validator's latest attestation.

It picks the head of the chain every slot. Gasper is the combination of LMD-GHOST fork choice with Casper FFG finality.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #66: If two versions of the chain compete, nodes follow the one most validators recently voted for. This rule picks the head of the chain every slot.

Only each validator's latest vote counts, so old votes can't be piled up. A second rule then locks in history every few minutes.

card.title: How nodes pick the head of the chain
card.sub: LMD-GHOST follows the branch with the most latest votes. Gasper adds finality.

long: Every active validator attests once per epoch. Each epoch, validators are shuffled into committees spread across the 32 slots, with a target committee size of 128 and up to 64 committees per slot, so the voting load is split. Each attestation votes for a head block plus source and target checkpoints, feeding both fork choice and finality.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #67: Every active validator attests once per epoch. Validators are shuffled into committees across the 32 slots (target committee size 128, up to 64 committees per slot), splitting the voting load.

Each attestation votes for a head block plus source and target checkpoints, feeding both fork choice and finality.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #67: Every active validator votes once per epoch (every 6.4 minutes). Validators are randomly split into small groups so no single block gets all the votes at once.

Each vote does double duty: it says which block is the current head, and which checkpoints should become final. One signature, two jobs.

card.title: Everyone votes once per epoch
card.sub: Validators are shuffled into committees across 32 slots to spread the load.

long: Block proposers are picked from RANDAO randomness, weighted by effective balance: a random draw weighted by stake. EIP-7917 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) makes the proposer lookahead deterministic and stores it in the beacon state, so the schedule is fixed in advance and visible on-chain, which helps preconfirmation designs.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #68: Block proposers are drawn from RANDAO randomness, weighted by effective balance. EIP-7917 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) makes the proposer lookahead deterministic and stores it in the beacon state.

The schedule is fixed in advance and visible on-chain, which helps preconfirmation designs.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #68: Who proposes the next block? A random draw weighted by stake. Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), the proposer schedule is fixed in advance and visible on-chain.

Knowing who proposes the next blocks lets new services promise users early that their transaction will be included, before the block even exists.

card.title: A stake-weighted lottery for proposers
card.sub: Since Fusaka, the proposer schedule is fixed in advance and visible on-chain.

long: The consensus layer signs with BLS12-381. BLS signatures on the same message can be aggregated into one 96-byte signature that verifies against the aggregate public key, so a whole committee's votes cost about one check. That's how Ethereum handles hundreds of thousands of validators voting every epoch.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #69: The consensus layer signs with BLS12-381. BLS signatures on the same message aggregate into one 96-byte signature that verifies against the aggregate public key.

A whole committee's votes cost about one check. That's how Ethereum handles hundreds of thousands of validators voting every epoch.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #69: Hundreds of thousands of validators vote every few minutes. Ethereum can handle it because their signatures can be squeezed together into one.

Instead of checking each vote separately, nodes check one combined signature for a whole group. Without this trick, the network would drown in signatures.

card.title: Many votes squeezed into one signature
card.sub: BLS signatures aggregate, so a whole committee's votes cost about one check.

long: Altair (Oct 2021) added sync committees: 512 validators, picked every 256 epochs (about 27 h), sign each beacon block header. A light client only has to verify one aggregate BLS signature to follow the chain, instead of processing the full beacon chain. That lets light wallets follow Ethereum without downloading it.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #70: Altair (Oct 2021) added sync committees: 512 validators, picked every 256 epochs (≈27 h), sign each beacon block header.

A light client only verifies one aggregate BLS signature to follow the chain, instead of processing the full beacon chain. That lets light wallets follow Ethereum without downloading it.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #70: Light wallets can follow Ethereum without downloading it, thanks to a small rotating group of 512 validators that sign every block header.

The group changes about once a day. A phone wallet only needs to check their combined signature to trust a header, then verify its balance against it.

card.title: Light clients follow a small committee
card.sub: A rotating group signs each header. Light wallets verify one aggregate signature.

long: Validators are slashed, losing part of their stake and being forced out, for signing conflicting messages. There are three slashable offenses: proposing two different blocks for the same slot, double voting (two attestations with the same target epoch) and surround voting (one vote's source-target span contains another's).
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #71: Validators are slashed, losing part of their stake and forced out, for signing conflicting messages. There are three slashable offenses.

Proposing two different blocks for the same slot; double voting (two attestations with the same target epoch); and surround voting (one vote's source-target span contains another's).
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #71: Validators who cheat get "slashed": part of their stake is destroyed and they are kicked out. Cheating means signing two conflicting blocks or votes.

Anyone can submit the two conflicting signatures as proof. Being offline is not cheating: it only costs small penalties. Lying is what gets punished hard.

card.title: Three ways to get slashed
card.sub: Double proposals, double votes and surround votes. Part of the stake is destroyed.

long: Slashing penalties have two parts. An initial cut, 1/4096 of effective balance since Pectra's EIP-7251 (was 1/32).
