Then, about 18 days later, a correlation penalty scaled by the total stake slashed around that time. A lone validator slashed by mistake loses little; in a mass slashing each validator can lose everything.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #72: Slashing penalties have two parts: an initial cut, 1/4096 of effective balance since Pectra's EIP-7251 (was 1/32), then ≈18 days later a correlation penalty scaled by the total stake slashed around that time.

A lone validator slashed by mistake loses little; in a mass slashing, each validator can lose everything.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #72: A lone validator slashed by mistake loses a small amount. But if many get slashed at the same time, each loses much more, possibly all its stake.

The logic: one validator misbehaving is probably a bug or a mistake. Many at once looks like a coordinated attack, and the penalty is sized to make attacks ruinous.

card.title: Slashing hurts most in a crowd
card.sub: A lone mistake costs little. In a mass slashing each validator can lose everything.

long: If more than 1/3 of stake is offline, the chain can't reach the 2/3 needed to finalize. After 4 epochs without finality, the inactivity leak starts: inactive validators' balances drain faster and faster. Their share of stake shrinks until active validators hold 2/3 again and finality resumes, however many went offline.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #73: If > 1/3 of stake is offline, the chain can't reach the 2/3 needed to finalize. After 4 epochs without finality, the inactivity leak starts: inactive validators' balances drain faster and faster.

Their share shrinks until active validators hold 2/3 again and finality resumes, however many went offline.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #73: If over a third of validators go offline, the chain stops finalizing. The offline ones then slowly lose stake until the active ones are back above two-thirds.

Blocks keep coming the whole time. Even if half the network disappeared in a disaster, Ethereum would eventually finalize again, on its own.

card.title: The inactivity leak restores finality
card.sub: Offline validators drain stake until active ones hold two-thirds again.

long: Validator rewards are built from a base reward proportional to effective_balance / sqrt(total active stake). Total issuance therefore grows with the square root of total stake, much slower than stake itself, and the yield per validator falls as more ETH is staked.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #74: Validator rewards are built from a base reward proportional to effective_balance / sqrt(total active stake).

Total issuance therefore grows with the square root of total stake, much slower than stake itself, and the yield per validator falls as more ETH is staked.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #74: The more ETH is staked, the less each validator earns in percentage terms. Total new ETH issued grows much slower than the amount staked.

Quadruple the stake and total issuance only doubles. It's a balance: enough reward to attract validators, without printing too much ETH.

card.title: More stake, lower yield per validator
card.sub: Rewards scale with one over the square root of total stake, so issuance grows slower.

long: Staked ETH could not be withdrawn at all until Shapella on April 12, 2023 (EIP-4895). Withdrawals need no transaction or gas: a sweep scans validators in order and adds up to 16 withdrawals to each block, either partial (balance above the cap) or full (exited validators). Rewards above the stake are paid out automatically.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #75: Staked ETH couldn't be withdrawn until Shapella on Apr 12, 2023 (EIP-4895). Withdrawals need no tx or gas: a sweep scans validators in order and adds up to 16 withdrawals to each block.

Either partial (balance above the cap) or full (exited validators). Rewards above the stake are paid out automatically.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #75: Staked ETH could not be withdrawn at all until April 12, 2023. Since then, rewards above the stake are paid out to validators' wallets automatically.

Early stakers locked their ETH for over two years with no exit. Now, the network sweeps through validators and pays out, with no transaction or fee needed.

card.title: Withdrawals arrive without a transaction
card.sub: Since Shapella in April 2023, a sweep pays out rewards automatically, no gas needed.

long: EIP-7251 (Pectra, May 7, 2025) raises MAX_EFFECTIVE_BALANCE from 32 to 2048 ETH for validators with 0x02 (compounding) withdrawal credentials; the minimum stays 32 ETH. Rewards above 32 can auto-compound, and validators can be consolidated, so large stakers need far fewer validators.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #76: EIP-7251 (Pectra, May 7, 2025) raises MAX_EFFECTIVE_BALANCE from 32 to 2048 ETH for validators with 0x02 (compounding) withdrawal credentials; the minimum stays 32 ETH.

Rewards above 32 can auto-compound, and validators can be consolidated, so large stakers need far fewer validators.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #76: A validator used to be capped at 32 ETH. Since May 2025, one validator can hold up to 2,048 ETH, so big stakers need far fewer of them.

Rewards can now stay inside and keep earning, instead of being swept out. And fewer validators means less voting traffic for the whole network.

card.title: Bigger validators, fewer of them
card.sub: Since Pectra, rewards can auto-compound and validators can be consolidated.

long: EIP-7002 (Pectra, May 2025) lets the withdrawal credential address trigger a validator's exit, or partial withdrawals, from the execution layer through a system contract, without the validator's signing key. Before, only the signing key could start an exit. Useful for staking pools and contracts that hold the withdrawal rights.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #77: EIP-7002 (Pectra, May 2025) lets the withdrawal credential address trigger a validator's exit, or partial withdrawals, from the execution layer through a system contract, without the validator's signing key.

Before, only the signing key could start an exit. Useful for staking pools and contracts that hold the withdrawal rights.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #77: Since May 2025, the wallet that receives a validator's withdrawals can also force it to exit. Before, only the validator's signing key could.

That matters when someone else runs your validator: if they disappear or misbehave, you no longer depend on them to get your ETH out.

card.title: Exits without the signing key
card.sub: Since Pectra, the withdrawal address can trigger exits. Useful for staking pools.

long: EIP-6110 (Pectra, May 2025) moves validator deposits in-protocol: the execution layer passes them directly to the consensus layer, replacing the old eth1 data voting. The delay between a deposit transaction and its processing drops from about 12 hours to about 13 minutes.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #78: EIP-6110 (Pectra, May 2025) moves validator deposits in-protocol: the execution layer passes them directly to the consensus layer, replacing the old eth1 data voting.

The delay between a deposit transaction and its processing drops from ≈12 hours to ≈13 minutes.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #78: A new staking deposit used to take about 12 hours just to be seen by the consensus layer. Since May 2025, that step takes about 13 minutes.

Before, validators had to vote on what they saw on the other layer, slowly. Now the deposit is handed over directly, inside the protocol.

card.title: Deposits seen in minutes, not hours
card.sub: EIP-6110 passes deposits straight from the execution layer to consensus.

long: Churn limits throttle how fast validators can join or leave, keeping the validator set stable and finality safe. EIP-7514 (Dencun) capped activations at 8 validators per epoch. Pectra (EIP-7251) replaced the count with an ETH-based churn, capped at 256 ETH per epoch, since validators can now hold up to 2048 ETH.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #79: Churn limits throttle how fast validators can join or leave, keeping the validator set stable and finality safe. EIP-7514 (Dencun) capped activations at 8 validators per epoch.

Pectra (EIP-7251) replaced the count with an ETH-based churn, capped at 256 ETH per epoch, since validators can now hold up to 2048 ETH.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #79: Validators can't all join or leave at once: there's a queue with a cap per epoch. It keeps the validator set stable and finality safe.

If a huge share of stake could exit in minutes, attacks on finality would get easier. The queue makes big changes take days or weeks.

card.title: A queue at the validator door
card.sub: Churn limits cap entries and exits per epoch, keeping finality safe.

long: Ethereum runs on several independent clients written by different teams. Per ethereum.org, a bug in a consensus client used by more than 1/3 of nodes could stop finality, and one with a 2/3 majority could finalize an invalid chain. Ideally no client exceeds 33%. With diversity, if one client has a bug, the others keep the chain going.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #80: Ethereum runs on several independent clients. Per ethereum.org, a bug in a consensus client used by > 1/3 of nodes could stop finality, and one with a 2/3 majority could finalize an invalid chain.

Ideally no client exceeds 33%. With diversity, if one client has a bug, the others keep the chain going.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #80: Ethereum runs on many independent software versions written by different teams. If one has a bug, the others keep the chain going.

The danger is concentration: if one version ran on two-thirds of validators and had a bug, it could lock in a broken chain. Spreading out is the defense.

card.title: Why client diversity matters
card.sub: A bug in a client used by over 1/3 of nodes could stop finality.

long: MEV-Boost (by Flashbots) is out-of-protocol proposer-builder separation. Many validators don't build their own blocks: specialized builders send blocks to relays, relays pick the most profitable one for the proposer, and the proposer's consensus client publishes it. This happens outside the core protocol.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #81: MEV-Boost (by Flashbots) is out-of-protocol proposer-builder separation. Specialized builders send blocks to relays, relays pick the most profitable one for the proposer, and its consensus client publishes it.

Many validators don't build their own blocks. This happens outside the core protocol.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #81: Many validators don't build their own blocks. They let specialized "builders" assemble them and pick the one that pays best. This happens outside the core protocol.

Builders compete to order transactions profitably and share the gains with validators. It raises income, but puts a lot of trust in a few relays and builders.

card.title: Who really builds the blocks
card.sub: With MEV-Boost, builders compete via relays and proposers pick the best payer.

long: EIP-4844 (Dencun, Mar 13, 2024) added blobs: type-3 transactions carry blobs of 4,096 field elements x 32 bytes = 131,072 bytes (128 KiB). The EVM can't read blob content, only a versioned hash of its KZG commitment. Blobs gave rollups a cheap data lane separate from calldata.
tech:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #82: EIP-4844 (Dencun, Mar 13, 2024) added blobs: type-3 txs carry blobs of 4,096 field elements × 32 bytes = 131,072 bytes (128 KiB).

The EVM can't read blob content, only a versioned hash of its KZG commitment. Blobs gave rollups a cheap data lane separate from calldata.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #82: Since March 2024, Ethereum has "blobs": big chunks of cheap data, about 128 KB each, used by rollups to post their transactions.

Contracts can't read what's inside, they only see a fingerprint. That's enough for rollups, and makes blobs much cheaper than regular transaction data.
variant:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #82: Layer 2 fees dropped sharply in March 2024. Why? Ethereum added "blobs", a cheap data lane built for rollups, each about 128 KB.

Before, rollups had to post their data as regular transaction data, the most expensive way. Blobs are kept only for a few weeks and priced separately.

card.title: Blobs, a data lane for rollups
card.sub: Since March 2024 rollups post data in blobs. The EVM sees only a commitment.

long: Blobs are not kept forever. Consensus nodes must serve blob data for 4096 epochs (about 18 days), then may prune it: MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_BLOB_SIDECARS_REQUESTS, and its data column equivalent since Fusaka's PeerDAS. That is long enough for anyone to check the data, while keeping nodes light. Only the commitment stays in blocks permanently.

The fingerprint of each blob stays in the chain for good. Anyone who wants the full data longer, like the rollup itself or archive services, can keep a copy.

card.sub: Long enough for anyone to check the data. Only the commitment stays forever.

long: EIP-4844 created a separate blob gas market with its own EIP-1559-style base fee, also burned. Each blob uses 2^17 = 131,072 blob gas. At Dencun the target was 3 blobs per block and the max 6. Because the markets are separate, blob fees can be near zero when few rollups need space, even if regular gas is expensive.

#Ethereum Deep Dive #84: Blobs have their own fee, separate from normal gas. When few rollups need space, blob fees can be close to zero even if regular gas is expensive.

It works like normal gas: when blocks have more blobs than the target, the blob fee rises; fewer, and it falls. The blob fee is burned too.

card.title: Blobs have their own fee market
card.sub: Blob fees can be near zero when demand is low, even if regular gas is expensive.

Anyone could contribute from a browser. For the setup to be broken, every single one of those 141,000 contributions would have to be dishonest.

card.title: A trusted setup with a crowd
card.sub: The KZG ceremony ran 208 days in 2023. One honest participant is enough.

More blob space means rollups compete less for room, which keeps their fees low as they grow. And the mini-upgrades that followed Fusaka kept raising the numbers.

card.title: Pectra doubled the blob target
card.sub: More room for rollups, and the baseline Fusaka built on.

long: PeerDAS (EIP-7594, Fusaka, activated Dec 3, 2025) is data availability sampling: blob data is erasure-coded and split, and each node only downloads and checks samples instead of every blob. Like spot-checking a book, sampling gives high confidence that the full data was published, without every node fetching all of it.

simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #87: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), nodes don't download every blob. They check random pieces, like spot-checking a book, and are confident the whole data was published.

The data is encoded so it can be rebuilt from part of it. If enough random pieces are there, the whole thing is. That lets blob space grow without heavier nodes.

card.title: Spot-checking instead of downloading
card.sub: PeerDAS lets nodes sample blob data and still be confident it was all published.

long: EIP-7892 created 'Blob Parameter Only' (BPO) forks: lightweight upgrades that change only blob parameters (target, max, base fee update fraction). Two followed Fusaka: BPO1 (Dec 9, 2025) set target/max to 10/15 and BPO2 (Jan 7, 2026) to 14/21, up from 6/9 at Fusaka activation. Blob capacity can rise without a full upgrade.

simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #88: Ethereum can now raise blob capacity with mini-upgrades that change only that setting. Two followed Fusaka: Dec 2025 and Jan 2026.

In a few weeks, the blob target went from 6 to 14 per block. Instead of waiting a year for a big upgrade, capacity can grow in small, safe steps.

card.title: Mini-upgrades for blob capacity
card.sub: BPO forks change only blob parameters. Two followed Fusaka, in Dec 2025 and Jan 2026.

long: Before Fusaka, the blob base fee could fall to 1 wei when demand was low, and rising again took a long time. EIP-7918 (Fusaka, Dec 2025) bounds the blob base fee by execution cost: when it is too low relative to the execution base fee, it stops falling. Blobs now pay a minimum linked to the price of regular gas.

simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #89: Blob fees used to fall to almost nothing, even when the network was busy. Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), blobs pay a minimum linked to the price of regular gas.

A near-zero fee meant it took ages to react when demand suddenly rose. A floor keeps the fee closer to reality, so it can adjust quickly.

card.title: A floor under blob fees
card.sub: Blob fees could fall to 1 wei. Now they have a minimum linked to regular gas.

long: EIP-7702 (Pectra, May 2025) adds type-4 transactions: an EOA signs an authorization that sets its code to 0xef0100 || address, a pointer to a contract. Calls to the EOA then run that code in its context, so a regular wallet can batch transactions, have gas sponsored or add spending rules without changing address. The delegate must be chosen with care.

A regular wallet can batch txs, have gas sponsored or add spending rules without changing address. Pick the delegate with care.
simple:
#Ethereum Deep Dive #90: Since May 2025, a regular wallet can act like a smart contract wallet: batch transactions, have someone else pay gas, add spending rules, without changing its address.

The wallet points to a contract whose code it borrows. Choose that contract carefully: a malicious one would get full control of your account.

card.title: Your wallet can borrow contract code
card.sub: EIP-7702 lets an EOA batch, get gas sponsored and add rules, same address.
